prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene at magic twist angles and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, opening the field of moiré quantum matter.

statement.case_for: Moiré quantum matter is the best fit to the 'discovery or invention' criterion among the shortlisted candidates. A concrete, quantitative prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) was tested seven years later by Jarillo-Herrero's group, which found correlated insulators and superconductivity, and the result was reproduced by several independent groups and carried into twisted TMDs, multilayers and fractional Chern insulators. The topic and the people responsible are identifiable, the three-person configuration is natural (two theorists of one prediction, one experimental leader), and eight years of independent confirmation make it mature enough. Four first-place votes and five top-three placements show it has the broadest support of any shortlisted candidate, and my own reasons for it are independent of that count. In my opening ballot I put aberration-corrected electron optics (B030) first. On reflection I think B001 should lead this year. B030 is the candidate I know best, which is a reason for me to discount my own enthusiasm rather than press it, since nobody else ranked it in their top eight.
statement.case_against: The origin of the superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene is still disputed, so the Nobel-relevant discovery is the flat-band prediction and the observation of the correlated phases, not a settled mechanism. The three-name limit forces choices. Cao and the other first-author experimentalists of the 2018 papers, the Fatemi/Dean-type independent experiments and earlier twisted-graphene theory (for example Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, and Suárez Morell et al.) have credit claims that I cannot resolve from the supplied names. The field is also still moving quickly, so a prize now risks freezing a story that later work may revise.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B001 first as a clean prediction-then-test case, with Bistritzer-MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero as the decisive pair, and acknowledges that other experimental groups have claims.
responses.response: I agree on the structure of the argument, and it is why I moved B001 to the top of my own list. I would qualify one point: the claims of other groups are not interchangeable. The independent experiments that confirmed the phases show robustness, and I treat them as evidence of maturity, not as an attribution problem. The real attribution risk is on the theory side, where earlier twisted-graphene band-structure work exists, and that is why the citation should name the continuum-model prediction of flat bands at magic angles and not 'twisted graphene' generally.

responses.point: Mehlig also puts B001 first but proposes a two-person prize for MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, noting that this is the cleanest configuration even though it leaves Bistritzer out.
responses.response: I disagree with dropping Bistritzer. The 2011 prediction is a two-author result, and the committee has room for three. Leaving out Bistritzer would break the attribution to make the prize look tidier, when the supplied names allow us to be accurate. I accept that a three-person B001 means that no second achievement can share the prize this year, and I think that is an acceptable cost.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock (B007) first as a clear invention that changed what can be measured, and stresses that Hall and Hänsch (2005) covered the comb, so Katori and Ye's clock role is separate.
responses.response: I take B007 seriously and kept it as an alternative. I agree that the lattice clock is a clean invention, and I also had it third. I accept the 2005 distinction, since the magic-wavelength idea is separable from the comb. Where I differ is on timing and on the 'invention' criterion for this year in particular. The redefinition of the second is still pending, so its formal impact is not yet realised, and Kroll's reading seems to count that anticipated impact as already done. I would not oppose B007 as a later or a combined prize, but it cannot share a prize with B001 under the three-person limit unless B001 is cut to two people.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B058) first, with Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf as theory and experiment, and notes that the supplied credit leaves out Andreas Wallraff, whose experiment was central.
responses.response: The omission of Wallraff is a serious attribution problem for B058 as shortlisted, and he cannot be added under the listed names. That, together with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, makes me hesitant to place B058 above B001 this year. I do not dispute its scientific weight. I would like Johansson to say whether he would still support B058 if the credit had to be limited to the three names as listed.

uncertainties: Whether the three credited names for B001 fairly represent the experimental credit, given the first authors and collaborators of the 2018 papers and the independent confirming groups.
How much weight to give earlier twisted-graphene band-structure theory when the citation is written.
Whether the unresolved mechanism of the superconductivity matters for a prize citation that is limited to flat bands and observed correlated phases.

My opening first-place candidate B030 has the Krivanek (STEM) attribution problem, which I cannot resolve from the credited names, and which the committee would need to judge independently of my familiarity with the field.
Whether B007 should be paired with another achievement in a later year, since a two-part prize with B001 is not possible within three people.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the B001 candidates from my profile. Two connections should be recorded. First, B030 (electron optics) lies in my own research field of electron microscopy and I have previously ranked it first, though my profile documents no personal relationship with Rose, Urban or Haider, and I would recuse myself from any decision on B030 if the committee judges that necessary. Second, I hold a University of Tokyo fellowship and have long-running exchanges with Japanese universities, which is a possible but undocumented link to B007 (Katori); I also share Chalmers with Göran Johansson, whose first-place candidate is B058, though I have no documented collaboration with him.
